generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, a placement or applied project offers what a seminar cannot: contact with real work, real settings and real decisions. A few weeks on a placement, in a studio, a laboratory or the field can build practical skills, strengthen your employability, and show you which part of your field actually suits you. The gains are real, but they come most fully to the student who arrives knowing what they want from the time.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students taking up the same month-long placement in their field.

Student A turns up each day, does the tasks given, and goes home. The work gets done. But Student A never decided what the placement was for, so it drifts: no goal to steer by, no sense of what to notice, nothing gathered beyond the hours logged. At the end there is little to show but attendance.

Student B starts the same placement with two or three clear aims: to learn how the setting really works, to build a particular skill, and to leave with examples for a future application. Those aims shape each day, what to volunteer for, what to ask, what to note. The same month yields skills, insight and evidence.

Both served the same time. Only Student B decided in advance what to draw from it, and so actually drew it.
generatedProse.summary: A practice or work-based experience offers real skills, employability and self-knowledge, but only to the student who aims for them. You can now identify what such an experience can give you, recognise the difference between drifting and drawing value, and set clear aims of your own. The next lesson turns those aims into action: the moves that get the most out of the experience while you are in it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's month more valuable than Student A's?

items.text: Student B set clear aims in advance, which shaped what they did, asked and gathered.
Student B was given more interesting tasks than Student A was.
Student B spent more hours on the placement than Student A did.
Student B was naturally more confident than Student A.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B set aims in advance, and those aims steered what they did, asked and gathered across the month.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B decided before the placement began.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's month was more valuable because of clear aims set in advance, which steered the whole placement, not because of better tasks, more hours or confidence.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
